text: Every video about the deep sea gives you the same list. The anglerfish. The gulper eel. The giant isopod. Eight animals, in the dark, one after another.
This isn't that list. Because down there, the animals aren't the point. The tricks are.
A thousand metres down, the water presses on you with about a hundred times the weight of the air at the surface. But that isn't the problem that shapes the animals.
Below a thousand metres there is no light, almost no food, and nowhere to hide — and every animal that lives there has solved that with one of a handful of strategies. Eight types.
Learn them, and you can look at any deep-sea creature and know what it's for.
Type one is the one you already know. You just don't know why it works.
Here's the deep-sea rule that explains almost everything in this video: food is so scarce that chasing it costs more energy than it gives back. So the first strategy is not to chase at all.
A female deep-sea anglerfish grows to about twenty centimetres. Above her mouth hangs a rod — a stretched-out fin spine — and on its tip, a glowing bulb. The light isn't hers.
Inside that bulb live bacteria that make their own light, and she gives them a home in exchange for the glow.
And she is not the only one glowing. NOAA estimates around ninety percent of the animals in the open water column make their own light. Down here, a light is not strange. A light that hangs still is.
In water where nothing else shines, a small moving light is the most interesting thing for hundreds of metres. Things come to look. She doesn't move.
And the males? About two point eight centimetres. A seventh of her length. He has no lure at all, and he doesn't glow.
Which creates the same problem the food does: in all that dark, how does he ever find her? In some species, the answer is that once he does, he never lets go.
He latches on — and over time, he fuses into her body, until he is a permanent part of her. Two animals, one bloodstream, one lure.
Type one: make the food come to you. Type two takes the same idea — and cheats.

Nearly every light in the deep sea is blue. Blue travels best through water, and blue is what deep-sea eyes evolved to see. Which means, down here, red light is effectively invisible: most animals simply cannot see it.
Three kinds of dragonfish — loose-jawed hunters called Malacosteus, Aristostomias and Pachystomias — have a second light under each eye that shines far-red, beyond seven hundred nanometres.
And they are among the very few animals down there that can see it.
So picture it. A hunter with a torch that only it can see, sweeping a beam across the dark, lighting up prey that has no idea it is lit.

One of them, Malacosteus, sees its own red light using a pigment related to chlorophyll — the green stuff in plants — which it seems to get from its food. A predator, a kilometre down, seeing by borrowed plant chemistry.
Two types down. The next one doesn't bother with light at all. It bets everything on one bite.
If a meal comes past once a week, you cannot afford to miss it. The gulper eel's answer: a mouth that cannot miss.
Its lower jaw is estimated to be a quarter the length of its entire body. It opens like a net and expands into a pouch — the same reason it's also called the pelican eel.

The rest of the animal is almost an afterthought: a thin tail, small eyes, a body that is barely there. Everything the eel is has been spent on the one thing that matters at this depth — never letting a meal get away.
And its skin is among the blackest in the ocean. When scientists on a NOAA expedition caught one in 2019, they measured it. A mouth with a shadow attached.
Type four goes the opposite way. Instead of being as black as possible — it disappears.
In the twilight zone there's nowhere to hide: no rock, no weed, no floor. Only water. So a whole class of animals hides in the one place left — inside the water itself, by being transparent.
Biologists call it hiding in plain sight, and it is especially common among animals of the open midwater, exactly where there is nothing to hide behind.
In 2023 a NOAA camera off Alaska filmed a glass squid, seven hundred metres down. Almost the whole animal is clear.
The only things you can see are what it can't make transparent: a small red digestive gland in the middle, and two pale gills either side of it. Everything else is water-coloured.

It is harder than it sounds. To be transparent, almost nothing inside you can scatter light — so the parts that have to be solid are kept small, and the rest is given up. It is a strategy that costs you a body.
Four types down. And the next one solves the food problem by being enormous.
You have met a relative of this animal. The pill bug — the little grey woodlouse that rolls into a ball under a flowerpot. Now imagine one a foot and a half long.
That's the giant isopod, Bathynomus giganteus. NOAA has filmed them on the sea floor around a thousand metres down, and eating whatever falls from above — including fish heads.
They live from a couple of hundred metres down to more than two thousand, in water of about four degrees. Fourteen legs, and — like the pill bug — it curls into a ball when bothered.
Even their eggs are oversized: just over a centimetre across, among the largest of any marine invertebrate, carried twenty or thirty at a time in a pouch under the mother.
Why so big? This is a pattern across the deep: animals in deep, cold water often grow much larger than their shallow-water relatives.
Biologists call it deep-sea gigantism. Why it happens is still argued: the usual suspects are the cold, the scarcity of food, and the slow metabolism that comes with both.
There are more than twenty species of these giants, and this one is the biggest. What isn't argued is that it happens.
And this particular giant has one more trick. The next type is the same animal — and what it can do when the food stops coming.
At Toba Aquarium in Japan, a giant isopod known as Number One arrived in 2007. In January 2009 it ate a meal. Then it stopped.
Keepers offered food for years. It refused all of it. It was found dead on the fourteenth of February, 2014 — more than five years after its last meal.
Number One was extreme, but not a freak: other captive giant isopods have gone years without eating, then gorged when food finally appeared.
And in the wild, when there's nothing to eat, they dig into the sediment and stay still — spending as little as possible until the next meal falls.
That is the sixth strategy, and it may be the most important of all down there: when food arrives once in a great while, you don't need to be fast, or clever, or bright. You need to be able to wait.
The deep sea is full of animals whose main talent is doing almost nothing, for an astonishingly long time, and then eating everything.
Six down. Now the strangest builder in the ocean.
A giant larvacean is a soft animal about five centimetres long — and it lives inside a house it builds itself, out of mucus.
Not a small house. Two net-like filters, one inside the other, and the outer one can be up to a metre across.
The animal sits at the centre and beats its tail, pulling water through: the outer net stops the coarse stuff, the inner net traps the tiny particles it actually eats.
When the filters clog, the larvacean abandons the whole house and builds another. The old one sinks — and not slowly. A discarded house can drop eight hundred metres in a single day.
Scientists call these houses "sinkers", and they carry carbon from the surface down into the deep sea in quantities that turned out to be a missing piece of the ocean's carbon budget.
A strategy of drifting, filtering, and throwing away your home. And it helps run the planet.
MBARI found that the same filters collect microplastic particles, and the larvaceans eat them — so the sinking houses are also a pathway carrying plastic into deep-sea food webs.
The drifters have a giant of their own, too.

In 2020, off Western Australia, a camera on the research ship Falkor found a siphonophore — a colony of thousands of tiny identical animals, each doing one job, strung together into a single drifting line — estimated at forty-five metres long.
If the estimate holds, it is the longest animal ever recorded. And it hunts by doing nothing: it hangs in the water like a curtain and waits for things to swim into it.
One type left — and it's the one that turns a death into a neighbourhood.

When a whale dies and sinks, it lands on a sea floor that has almost never seen that much food at once. Everything comes. And when the flesh is gone, and only the skeleton is left — something arrives that eats bone.
They're called Osedax. Worms, found on a whale skeleton nearly three kilometres down on the floor of Monterey Bay, and named in 2004. They have no way to chew.
Instead, the females grow branching, root-like tissues into the bone, and inside those roots live bacteria that break down the fats and oils locked in whale bone — directly — and feed the worm.
When scientists described it, it was the first time anyone had seen a fat-digesting bacterium living inside another animal this way.
And the males? They are dwarfs — microscopic, living inside the jelly tube around her body — and some of the larger species have been found with more than six hundred of them.
In a world where meeting a mate is as unlikely as finding a meal, the answer is to bring the whole population to the bone.

Scientists have since found thirty-two species, from ten metres down to four thousand — and not only on whales. Fish, birds, turtles, even land mammals. Wherever a skeleton lands, something is waiting for it.
They aren't alone. Bone-eating snails share the same skeleton. The scavengers strip the soft tissue in a matter of months; the skeleton then feeds a community for years — sometimes decades.
That's the eighth strategy: don't wait for crumbs. Wait for the whole meal, once — and then build your life on it.
Eight types. The lure. The red torch. The trap mouth. The glass body. The giant. The faster. The drifter. The bone-eater.
Eight answers to the same three problems: no light, no food, nowhere to hide.
So the next time you see one of these animals — on a screen, in a list, in a museum — don't ask what it is. Ask which trick it's using. You'll usually be able to tell.
